text_blocks.snippet: The three-dimensional double-helix structure of DNA was formally discovered and proposed by James Watson and Francis Crick in April 1953.
James Watson and Francis Crick: Built the physical model that solved the double-helix structure at the University of Cambridge. They shared the 1962 Nobel Prize for the discovery.

Rosalind Franklin: Captured "Photograph 51," a critical X-ray diffraction image of DNA that provided essential data for the double-helix model. Her colleague showed this data to Watson and Crick without her knowledge.
Maurice Wilkins: Worked with X-ray diffraction at King's College London and shared Franklin's data with Watson, later sharing the Nobel Prize with Watson and Crick.
Erwin Chargaff: Discovered that the amounts of adenine and thymine in DNA are equal, as are cytosine and guanine, which provided the rule for base pairing.
Friedrich Miescher: First identified DNA (which he called "nuclein") in white blood cells in 1869.
If you'd like, I can share more details about Photograph 51 or how base pairing works in the double helix.

perspectives.author: stem357
perspectives.title: Rosalind Franklin was a pioneering scientist whose work was crucial to the discovery of the DNA double helix. Using X-ray crystallography, she captured images of DNA's structure, including the famous "Photo 51," which provided key insights into the molecule's helical shape. However, without her knowledge or consent, her colleague Maurice Wilkins shared this data with James Watson and Francis Crick, who used it to build their model of DNA. While Watson and Crick were awarded the Nobel Prize for the discovery, Franklin’s contributions were largely overlooked during her lifetime. perspectives.author: interestingpedia
perspectives.title: Rosalind Franklin’s contribution to discovering the structure of DNA transformed modern biology, yet her role remained overshadowed for decades. Her X-ray diffraction image, famously known as *Photo 51*, provided crucial evidence for the DNA double helix. While James Watson and Francis Crick went on to publish the model and later receive the Nobel Prize, Franklin’s contribution received little recognition during her lifetime. She died in 1958 at the age of 37, and because Nobel Prizes are not awarded posthumously, she was never considered for the honour. Today, Rosalind Franklin is widely recognised as one of the most important scientists in the history of molecular biology—a reminder that groundbreaking discoveries are often built on the work of people history initially overlooks.

perspectives.author: themillionairewomensclub
perspectives.title: For six years, Rosalind Franklin carried a discovery that had the power to transform biology forever. In 1952, her remarkable work on Photo 51 provided one of the clearest views of DNA's helical structure and became a cornerstone of modern genetics. Despite the significance of her contribution, recognition did not come easily. Her marriage ended under public scrutiny, and she faced professional and personal challenges that would have discouraged many from continuing their scientific journey. Franklin remained committed to research and continued producing groundbreaking work in virology and molecular science. Her dedication to discovery never wavered, even when faced with criticism, injustice, and the lack of acknowledgment she deserved during her lifetime. She passed away from ovarian cancer at only thirty seven years old, but her legacy continues to inspire generations of scientists.
